title: A Protein Label Does Not Tell the Whole Food Story
summary:
Would adding protein turn a cookie into a healthier food? Not automatically, says dietician Daphene Altema-Johnson in a Smithsonian report about the protein craze.

Protein is important. Your body breaks it into small building blocks called amino acids, then uses those pieces to make its own proteins. People use 20 kinds of amino acids. Nine must come from food.

And muscles are only part of the story. Many hormones are proteins. So are antibodies, which help fight infections, and enzymes, which help with jobs such as digestion.

But the amount someone needs depends on their health, goals and food choices. People doing intense muscle-building workouts may benefit from more. Others may already get enough.

Teresa Fung, a nutrition researcher, explains that the body cannot simply keep a store of spare protein. Amino acids it cannot use are turned into energy.

The report discusses adult dietary guidelines, not a protein target for children. Its useful question is about the whole food, not just the biggest word on the package. Extra protein does not automatically improve everything else inside.
why_it_matters: Protein has many jobs in the body. Understanding those jobs and the food around it helps explain why a protein label does not describe a food’s whole nutritional value.

How many types of amino acids do people use?

They are stored as spare antibodies
They are stored as spare protein

options: It removes all the other nutrients in the cookie
It does not automatically make the cookie healthier
It automatically makes the cookie healthier
It replaces every other ingredient in the cookie

Explains amino acids and several jobs of proteins.
Discusses differing needs and the limits of a package label.

perspectives.description: Says adding protein does not automatically make a cookie or pastry healthier.
Explains that protein does more than make muscle and that the body cannot simply store spare protein.
